newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraqi sanctions retained intact after U.N. review.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi sanctions retained intact after U.N. review.

text.p: The Security Council, still not satisfied it has a full accounting of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, on Thursday retained intact the sanctions imposed on Baghdad soon after its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
"The regime is going to remain as it is," council President Park Soo Gil, South Korea's U.N. ambassador, told reporters after a review of the sanctions conducted every 60 days.

The sanctions, which include a ban on regular Iraqi oil sales, have remained unchanged since they were first enacted, except for a special arrangement that went into effect last December allowing Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food and medicine to help alleviate the plight of its people.

The main condition for any easing of sanctions is a clean bill of health from the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's chemical, biological and ballistic missile stocks and capability. The Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency performs a similar function monitoring Iraq's nuclear potential.

UNSCOM's chief, Rolf Ekeus, in his latest report in early April, said remaining questions about Baghdad's arms potential "requires the major political decision by Iraq's leadership to give up, once and for all, all capabilities and ambition to retain or acquire the proscribed weapons."

The council's review coincided with the announcement that Ekeus would leave his U.N. post on June 30 and would be succeeded as UNSCOM's executive chairman on July 1 by Australian U.N. ambassador Richard Butler.
Ekeus is expected to be appointed Sweden's ambassador in Washington.

Ambassador Edward Gnehm of the United States told his council colleagues during the sanctions review that the past two months had shown "no significant movement by Iraq towards fulfilling its obligations."
Gnehm, whose remarks were later made public, said: "I cannot say that Iraq is any closer to seeing the sanctions lifted than it appeared at the first review I attended ... in May 1994."

Iraq believed it need only satisfy UNSCOM's requirements to get the oil embargo lifted, he said, adding: "This is the reason it continues, as it has for six years, to ignore stolen property, missing persons and other vital issues."
He was referring to the return of property seized when Iraqi troops invaded Kuwait and the need to account for several hundred Kuwaitis and others whose fate is still unknown.
Gnehm said Iraq was "not yet convinced that the council cares about these issues. And sanctions will not be lifted until they are adequately addressed."
